page: Vultr vx1-g-192c-768g is a dedicated cloud compute instance in the VX1 Cloud Compute series. The system is driven by dedicated AMD x86_64 processors delivering 192 vCPUs alongside 768 GB of system memory. This configuration maintains a 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio, providing 4 GB of memory per core. The instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address and operates without discrete hardware GPU acceleration.

A key structural characteristic of this instance is its storage configuration. The server includes a 1 GB local NVMe SSD, which is strictly minimal. Because 1 GB is insufficient for modern operating systems and data retention, this instance requires integration with network-attached block storage or remote storage services for persistent execution environments and application workloads.

Without benchmark telemetry available, evaluation relies directly on the hardware profile. The presence of 192 dedicated physical cores prevents noisy-neighbor resource contention, while the 768 GB memory footprint accommodates substantial memory states. From a cost-efficiency perspective, the instance provides high compute density per instance deployment, best fitting parallel batch processing, distributed continuous integration, and in-memory analytics operating against centralized network storage.
description: Vultr vx1-g-192c-768g is a dedicated compute instance from the VX1 Cloud Compute line, built on AMD x86_64 architecture. It provides 192 dedicated vCPUs and 768 GB of system RAM, maintaining a standard general-purpose allocation ratio of 4 GB memory per vCPU. Hardware GPU acceleration is not present. Local physical storage is configured as a minimal 1 GB NVMe SSD, accompanied by one complimentary public IPv4 address. Because the integrated NVMe drive is constrained to 1 GB, operational environments require external network storage or attached block storage volumes to support persistent operating systems, data sets, and logging. With 192 dedicated AMD cores and massive overall memory capacity, this server profile suits large-scale parallel compute workloads, in-memory caching systems, distributed microservice infrastructure, and high-throughput application backends that utilize decoupled storage architectures.
